name: Logic and Discrete Math
author: Recurse
subject: math
description: Truth tables, logic gates, implications, quantifiers, counting, proofs, binary and modular arithmetic, and graphs.

lesson.intro: Discrete math is the math of separate, countable things: true and false statements, sets, arrangements and whole numbers. It is the language of proofs and the foundation of computer science.
objectives: Build truth tables and negate compound statements with De Morgan's laws
Tell an implication from its converse, inverse and contrapositive, and negate quantifiers
Count with sets, permutations, combinations and the pigeonhole principle
Recognize direct proof, contradiction and induction, and spot a broken proof
Convert between binary, decimal and hex, use remainders, and reason about graphs

sections.title: Propositions and truth tables
sections.key: AND is true only when both parts are true, OR when at least one is; to negate either, negate each part and flip the connective (De Morgan).
sections.body:
A **proposition** is a statement that is either true or false: "7 is prime" (true), "10 is odd" (false). "Close the door", "Is it raining?" and "x > 3" (until you know x) are not propositions.

**Connectives** combine them: NOT `¬P`, AND `P ∧ Q`, and OR `P ∨ Q`, which is inclusive: true when both parts are. A **truth table** lists every combination, and n variables give 2ⁿ rows.

[[visual]]

**De Morgan's laws** negate AND and OR: negate each part and flip the connective.

[[visual 2]]

Every chip runs this algebra with **logic gates**, tiny circuits that compute a connective with 1 for true and 0 for false.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Truth table
visual.caption: ¬P simply flips P: T becomes F and F becomes T.

visual.title: Logic gates
rows: Exactly one input is 1: "one or the other but not both"
Not both inputs are 1. Universal: every other gate can be built from NAND alone

sections.pitfall: Reading "or" as exclusive. In logic and in programming, P ∨ Q is also true when both parts are true; "one or the other but not both" is XOR.

activity.title: Truth tables in silicon
activity.prompt: Toggle the inputs through AND, OR and XOR and compare their outputs row by row: XOR differs from OR in exactly one row, the one where both inputs are 1. Then fill in the truth table for the target gate, and try building XOR from simpler gates.

check.question: When is P ∨ Q false?
choices: When exactly one of P and Q is true
Only when P and Q are both false
Only when P and Q are both true
Whenever P is false
check.explanation: Inclusive OR is true when at least one part is true, so its only false row is the one where both parts are false. "Exactly one is true" describes exclusive or, which is a different connective.

sections.title: Implication and the contrapositive
sections.key: `P → Q` is false only when P is true and Q is false; its contrapositive `¬Q → ¬P` always agrees with it, but its converse does not.
sections.body:
The **implication** `P → Q` reads "if P, then Q": P is the hypothesis and Q the conclusion. It promises something only when P is true, so it is false in exactly one case. When P is false the promise is never tested, so the implication counts as **vacuously true**.

[[visual]]

From one implication you can build three related statements, and only one of them is guaranteed to agree:

[[visual 2]]

To **negate** an implication, describe the case that breaks it: the negation of `P → Q` is `P ∧ ¬Q`. The negation of "If you study, you pass" is "You study and you do not pass".

visual.title: When is P → Q true?
rows: Promise broken: the only false row

visual.title: "If it is a dog, then it is a mammal"
rows: If it is a dog, it is a mammal
If it is a mammal, it is a dog
If it is not a dog, it is not a mammal
If it is not a mammal, it is not a dog

sections.pitfall: Assuming the converse. "If it rained, the street is wet" does not let you conclude "the street is wet, so it rained"; a street sweeper could have passed. Only the contrapositive is safe.

check.question: What is the contrapositive of "If n is even, then n² is even"?
choices: If n² is even, then n is even
If n is not even, then n² is not even
n is even and n² is not even
If n² is not even, then n is not even
check.explanation: The contrapositive swaps the two parts and negates both: ¬Q → ¬P. "If n² is even, then n is even" is the converse, "If n is not even, then n² is not even" is the inverse, and "n is even and n² is not even" is the negation.

sections.title: Quantifiers: for all and there exists
sections.key: To negate a quantified claim, swap ∀ and ∃ and push the NOT inside: the negation of "all passed" is "at least one did not pass".
sections.body:
A **predicate** is a statement with a variable, like P(x): "x is even". A **quantifier** says how many x are meant:

- `∀x P(x)` ("for all"): P(x) holds for every x in the domain.
- `∃x P(x)` ("there exists"): at least one x makes P(x) true.

The domain matters: `∀x (x² ≥ x)` is true over the integers but false over the reals, since x = 0.5 gives 0.25.

One **counterexample** disproves a "for all" claim: the number 2 sinks "every prime is odd". One example proves a "there exists" claim. But examples never prove a "for all" claim over an infinite domain.

[[visual]]

With two quantifiers, order changes the meaning:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Negating quantifiers
rows: At least one server is down

items.title: ∀x ∃y
points: Everyone loves somebody, possibly a different somebody each
`∀x ∃y (y > x)` over the integers: true, every number has a bigger one

items.title: ∃y ∀x
points: There is one person everybody loves: a far stronger claim
`∃y ∀x (y > x)` over the integers: false, no integer beats them all

sections.pitfall: Negating "all students passed" as "all students failed". The negation needs only one student who did not pass: ∃x ¬P(x).

check.question: What is the negation of "every integer is even or positive"?
choices: Every integer is odd and not positive
Some integer is odd or not positive
No integer is even or positive
Some integer is odd and not positive
check.explanation: ¬∀x (E(x) ∨ P(x)) becomes ∃x ¬(E(x) ∨ P(x)), and De Morgan turns the inside into ¬E(x) ∧ ¬P(x): some integer is odd and not positive (−3 is one). "Every integer is odd and not positive" negates the parts but forgets to swap ∀ for ∃.

sections.title: Sets and counting
sections.key: Count a union by adding sizes and subtracting the overlap; use permutations when order matters and combinations when it does not.
sections.body:
A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Take A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}:

[[visual]]

To count a union, subtract the overlap you counted twice: `|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|`, here 3 + 3 − 2 = 4.

The **multiplication principle**: m options followed by n options give m × n, so 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants make 12 outfits. For arrangements, ask whether order matters:

[[visual 2]]

The **pigeonhole principle** proves surprising facts with no calculation: put more than n items into n boxes and some box gets at least two. Among any 13 people, two share a birth month; among 367, two share a birthday, even counting February 29. A hash table with more keys than buckets must have a collision.

visual.title: Set operations
rows: In A but not in B
Every element of A is also in C

items.title: Permutation
points: Gold, silver and bronze among 10 runners: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

items.title: Combination
points: A 3-person committee from 10: each group appears 3! = 6 times among the 720, so 720 / 6 = 120

sections.pitfall: Using permutations when order does not matter, or the reverse. Ask whether rearranging the chosen items makes a different outcome: for a ranking, yes; for a committee or a poker hand, no.

check.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is A ∩ B?
check.explanation: The intersection keeps only elements that are in both sets: 3 and 4. {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is the union, and {1, 2} is A − B.

sections.title: Proof techniques
sections.key: Direct proof reasons forward from the hypothesis, contradiction assumes the opposite and reaches an impossibility, and induction needs a base case plus an inductive step.
sections.body:
A **proof** shows a statement must be true, with no exceptions. Examples are not enough: `n² + n + 41` is prime for every n from 0 to 39, then fails at n = 40, where it equals 41².

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Proving the contrapositive, `¬Q → ¬P`, is a close cousin of contradiction.

[[visual 3]]

Skip the base case and nothing has been shown true: the dominoes are set up, but none was ever pushed.

items.title: Direct proof
points: Assume the hypothesis and reason forward to the conclusion
Even + even is even: 2a + 2b = 2(a + b), twice a whole number

items.title: Contradiction
points: Show that leads to something impossible
So the statement must be true

items.title: Induction
points: **Inductive step**: if true for n = k, then true for n = k + 1
Like dominoes: the first falls and each knocks over the next

steps.label: So p² is even, so p is even
Lowest terms cannot have both parts even
Assume it holds for n = k
That is the claim for n = k + 1

sections.pitfall: Treating examples as proof. Checking n² + n + 41 from n = 0 to 39 looked convincing and was still wrong at 40. Examples can disprove a "for all" claim, never prove one.

check.question: In a proof by induction, what does the inductive step show?
choices: The claim holds for n = 1
The claim holds for many tested values of n
If the claim holds for n = k, it also holds for n = k + 1
Assuming the claim is false leads to a contradiction
check.explanation: The inductive step is the link between neighbors: true for k forces true for k + 1. Showing the claim for n = 1 is the base case, and testing many values is not a proof at all.

sections.title: Binary and modular arithmetic
sections.key: Binary places are powers of 2, one hex digit is exactly 4 bits, and `a mod n` is the remainder when a is divided by n.
sections.body:
**Binary** is base 2: each place is a power of 2, so `1011 = 1·8 + 0·4 + 1·2 + 1·1 = 11`. With n bits you can write 2ⁿ values, 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, so 8 bits cover 0 to 255.

[[visual]]

**Hexadecimal** is base 16, with digits 0 to 9 then A to F for 10 to 15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so group bits in fours from the right. Colors (#FF8800) and memory addresses (0x7ffe) are written this way.

[[visual 2]]

**Modular arithmetic** works with remainders: `a mod n` is the remainder of a ÷ n. `17 mod 5 = 2`, since `17 = 3·5 + 2`, written `17 ≡ 2 (mod 5)`. A clock works mod 12: 5 hours after 9 o'clock is 14 mod 12 = 2 o'clock.

Reduce at every step of a sum or product to keep the numbers small:

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: 13 to binary: divide by 2 repeatedly
visual.result: Read the remainders from last to first: `1101`

visual.title: Last digit of 7⁴: work mod 10
visual.caption: Remainders of powers repeat in a cycle, which tames huge exponents. Days of the week work mod 7.

sections.deeper:
**Remainders run computing.** A hash table picks a bucket with key mod table size. Check digits on barcodes and ISBNs catch typos with a remainder. Public-key cryptography such as RSA does its arithmetic mod a huge number.

**Repeating cycles.** Powers mod n repeat, which makes huge exponents easy. The last digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1, so 3¹⁰⁰ ends in 1 because 100 is a multiple of 4. Days of the week are mod 7: 100 days is 14 weeks and 2 days.
sections.pitfall: Reading binary from the wrong end. The rightmost bit is the 1s place; when converting by repeated division, read the remainders from the last one back to the first.

activity.title: Build numbers from bits
activity.prompt: Flip bits to hit each target. Start from the largest place value that fits and work right, the way you make change with the biggest coins first. Keep an eye on the hex readout: each group of 4 bits becomes one hex digit.

check.question: What is 23 mod 7?
check.explanation: 23 = 3 × 7 + 2, so the remainder is 2. 3 is the quotient, not the remainder, and 16 is 23 − 7, which takes away only one 7.

sections.title: Graphs and trees
sections.key: The degrees of a graph's vertices add up to twice its number of edges, and a tree (connected, no cycles) with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.
sections.body:
A map app finding a route, a social network suggesting friends and a build tool ordering its steps all work on a **graph**: **vertices** joined by **edges**. A vertex's **degree** is the number of edges touching it.

[[visual]]

The **handshake lemma**: degrees add up to twice the number of edges, because each edge has two ends. So 5 people each shaking exactly 3 hands is impossible: 15 is odd.

[[visual 2]]

A **tree** is a connected graph with no cycles, and with n vertices it has exactly n − 1 edges. Add an edge and you create a cycle; remove one and it splits in two. File systems, family trees and Ethernet's spanning tree protocol rely on this.

An **Euler path** uses every edge exactly once. A connected graph has one only when zero or two vertices have odd degree.

visual.title: A graph with 5 vertices and 6 edges
visual.caption: Degrees: 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 12 = 2 × 6 edges. Four odd-degree vertices (B, C, D, E), so no Euler path.

visual.title: Graph vocabulary
rows: Edges have a direction: one-way streets, follows on a social network
Edges go both ways: mutual friendships
Edges carry numbers such as distances or costs
A sequence of vertices joined by edges
A path that returns to its start without reusing an edge
A path joins every pair of vertices

sections.deeper:
**Where graph theory began.** In 1736 Leonhard Euler asked whether someone could walk through Königsberg crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. Treat the four land masses as vertices and the bridges as edges: all four had odd degree, so no Euler path exists.

**Why trees have n − 1 edges.** Build a tree one vertex at a time: each new vertex joins with exactly one new edge. Start with 1 vertex and 0 edges, and you always have one fewer edge than vertices. So a connected graph with 10 vertices and 12 edges has extra edges, and each extra edge closes a cycle.
sections.pitfall: Assuming every connected graph is a tree. A tree also needs no cycles, which forces exactly n − 1 edges; a connected graph with more edges than that must contain a cycle.

check.question: A tree has 12 vertices. How many edges does it have?
check.explanation: A tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges, so 12 vertices means 11 edges. With 12 edges there would be a cycle, and 66 = C(12, 2) is the edge count of a complete graph where every pair is joined.

keyTerms.definition: A statement that is either true or false.
¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q: to negate, negate each part and flip AND and OR.
For P → Q, the statement ¬Q → ¬P, which is always logically equivalent to the original.
An arrangement where order matters; P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!.
A selection where order does not matter; C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!).
Assuming a statement is false and deriving something impossible, which shows the statement is true.
Proving a base case and that truth for k implies truth for k + 1, which proves a claim for every n.
Arithmetic on remainders; a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n.
∀ (for all) or ∃ (there exists): says whether a predicate must hold for every element of the domain or for at least one.
If more than n items go into n boxes, at least one box holds two or more items.
A set of vertices joined by edges; the degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it.
A connected graph with no cycles; a tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.

summary: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; the contrapositive agrees, the converse may not.
To negate AND or OR, negate each part and flip the connective; "not all" means "at least one not".
Permutations when order matters, combinations when not; more items than boxes forces a shared box.
Induction needs a base case and an inductive step; contradiction assumes the opposite.
Binary places are powers of 2, a hex digit is 4 bits, and a mod n is the remainder.
Degrees add up to twice the edges, and a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why "if it is not a mammal, it is not a dog" says exactly the same thing as "if it is a dog, it is a mammal", while "if it is a mammal, it is a dog" does not.

questions.question: Which statement is equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
choices: ¬P ∨ ¬Q
¬P ∧ ¬Q
P ∨ Q
¬P ∧ Q
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law: negating an AND gives an OR of the negations. ¬P ∧ ¬Q is too strong; it claims both are false, while ¬(P ∧ Q) only says they are not both true. With P true and Q false, ¬(P ∧ Q) is true but ¬P ∧ ¬Q is false.

questions.question: A rule says: deny entry if NOT (age ≥ 18 OR has a permit). Which condition is equivalent?
choices: age < 18 OR no permit
age ≤ 18 AND no permit
age < 18 AND has a permit
age < 18 AND no permit
questions.explanation: By De Morgan, NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). NOT (age ≥ 18) is age < 18, and NOT (has a permit) is no permit. age ≤ 18 would wrongly deny 18-year-olds.

questions.question: When is the implication P → Q false?
choices: When P is false and Q is true
When P is true and Q is false
When P and Q are both false
Whenever Q is false
questions.explanation: An implication only breaks its promise when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. If P is false, the implication is vacuously true. "Whenever Q is false" misses that the row with P false and Q false is true.

questions.question: "If a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle" is true. Which statement must also be true?
choices: If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square
If a shape is not a rectangle, then it is not a square
If a shape is not a square, then it is not a rectangle
Some squares are not rectangles
questions.explanation: The contrapositive (not a rectangle → not a square) is always equivalent to the original. The converse (rectangle → square) fails for a 2 × 5 rectangle, and so does the inverse (not a square → not a rectangle).

questions.question: Why is "if P, then Q" counted as true when P is false?
questions.answer: The implication only promises something about cases where P is true. When P is false the promise is never tested, so it cannot have been broken; the statement is vacuously true.
questions.explanation: "If you score 100, I will buy you lunch" is not a lie if you score 80 and get no lunch. Only scoring 100 and getting no lunch breaks it, which matches the single false row of the truth table.

questions.question: What is the negation of "If it rains, the game is canceled"?
choices: If it does not rain, the game is not canceled
If it rains, the game is not canceled
It does not rain and the game is canceled
It rains and the game is not canceled
questions.explanation: The negation of P → Q is P ∧ ¬Q, the one situation that makes the original false. "If it rains, the game is not canceled" is just another implication; on a dry day both it and the original are vacuously true, so it cannot be the negation.

questions.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and B = {4, 5, 6, 7}. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
questions.explanation: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 5 + 4 − 2 = 7. The union is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Answering 9 counts 4 and 5 twice.

questions.question: In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded among 8 runners?
questions.explanation: Order matters, so this is a permutation: 8 choices for gold, then 7 for silver, then 6 for bronze: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. C(8, 3) = 56 would treat the three medals as identical.

questions.question: In how many ways can a 3-person committee be chosen from 8 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: C(8, 3) = (8 × 7 × 6) / 3! = 336 / 6 = 56. Each committee appears 6 times among the 336 ordered lists, so divide by 6.

questions.question: Which situation calls for combinations rather than permutations?
choices: Choosing 5 cards for a poker hand
Setting a 4-digit PIN with no repeated digits
Ranking the top 3 finishers in a race
Electing a president, a treasurer and a secretary
questions.explanation: A poker hand is the same hand in any order, so you count combinations. A PIN, a ranking and distinct officer roles all change when the order changes, so they are permutations.

questions.question: To prove √2 is irrational, you suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms and show p and q must both be even. Which technique is this?
choices: Direct proof
Proof by induction
Proof by contradiction
Proof by cases
questions.explanation: You assume the opposite of the claim (that √2 is rational) and reach an impossibility (a fraction in lowest terms with both parts even). That is proof by contradiction. A direct proof would start from the hypothesis and argue forward to the claim.

questions.question: An induction argument shows that "true for n = k" implies "true for n = k + 1", but never checks a base case. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; the inductive step alone proves the claim
The claim is then proved only for even n
Nothing has been shown true, so the chain never starts
The claim is proved for every n except n = 1
questions.explanation: The inductive step only says each domino knocks over the next; without a base case, no domino ever falls. The false claim "n = n + 1" has a valid inductive step (add 1 to both sides) but no true base case.

questions.question: What is the difference between a direct proof and a proof by contradiction?
questions.answer: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and reasons forward to the conclusion. A proof by contradiction assumes the conclusion is false and shows this leads to something impossible, so the conclusion must be true.
questions.explanation: Direct: 2a + 2b = 2(a + b) shows the sum of two evens is even. Contradiction suits claims like "√2 is irrational" or "there are infinitely many primes", where assuming the opposite gives you something concrete to work with.

questions.question: What is the binary number 101101 in decimal?
questions.explanation: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 1s sit at 32, 8, 4 and 1, so the value is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

questions.question: Write 25 in binary.
questions.explanation: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1. The places 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 get the digits 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, so 25 is 11001. Repeated division by 2 gives remainders 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, which read upward give the same answer.

questions.question: It is 10 o'clock. What hour will a 12-hour clock show 30 hours later?
questions.explanation: 10 + 30 = 40, and 40 mod 12 = 4 because 40 = 3 × 12 + 4. The clock shows 4 o'clock.

questions.question: What is the last digit of 3¹⁰⁰?
questions.explanation: Work mod 10. The last digits of powers of 3 repeat every 4 steps: 3, 9, 7, 1, 3, 9, ... Since 100 mod 4 = 0, 3¹⁰⁰ ends the same way as 3⁴ = 81, in 1.

questions.question: Match each piece of logic notation to its meaning.

pairs.right: P(x) holds for at least one x

questions.explanation: ¬, ∧ and ∨ are the basic connectives, → is implication, and ∀ and ∃ are the two quantifiers. ∨ is inclusive: it is also true when both parts are true.

questions.question: When does A XOR B output 1?
choices: When both A and B are 1
When exactly one of A and B is 1
When at least one of A and B is 1
When neither A nor B is 1
questions.explanation: XOR, exclusive or, is 1 when the inputs differ. "At least one is 1" describes OR, which is also 1 when both inputs are 1; that one row is the whole difference between them.

questions.question: Which single fact disproves the claim "every prime number is odd"?
choices: 9 is odd and not prime
There are infinitely many primes
2 is prime and even
Most even numbers are not prime
questions.explanation: A "for all" claim falls to one counterexample, and 2 is a prime that is not odd. 9 being odd and not prime says nothing about whether all primes are odd.

questions.question: What is the negation of "every server in the cluster is online"?
choices: Every server in the cluster is offline
No server in the cluster is online
At least one server in the cluster is online
At least one server in the cluster is offline
questions.explanation: ¬∀x Online(x) ≡ ∃x ¬Online(x): one offline server is enough to make the original false. "Every server is offline" is far stronger than the negation; it is the opposite extreme, not the denial.

questions.question: Over the integers, which statement is true?
choices: ∃y ∀x (y > x)
∀x ∃y (y > x)
∀x ∀y (y > x)
∃x ∀y (y > x)
questions.explanation: ∀x ∃y (y > x) says every integer has a bigger one, which is true (take y = x + 1). ∃y ∀x (y > x) claims one integer beats them all, including itself, which is false. Swapping the order of ∀ and ∃ changes the meaning.

questions.question: What is the smallest number of people that guarantees two of them were born in the same month?
questions.explanation: There are 12 months (boxes). With 12 people everyone could have a different month, but a 13th person must land in a month already taken. That is the pigeonhole principle.

questions.question: A graph has 7 edges. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
questions.explanation: By the handshake lemma, the degrees add up to twice the number of edges, since each edge has two ends: 2 × 7 = 14. This holds no matter how the edges are arranged.

questions.question: A connected graph has 10 vertices and 12 edges. What must be true?
choices: It is a tree
Some vertex has degree 0
It contains at least one cycle
It has an Euler path
questions.explanation: A connected graph with 10 vertices and no cycles would be a tree with exactly 9 edges. With 12 edges it must contain a cycle. Being connected rules out a degree-0 vertex, and an Euler path depends on the odd-degree count, which these numbers do not tell you.

questions.question: Write the binary number 1111 1010 in hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: Group the bits in fours: 1111 is 15, which is F, and 1010 is 10, which is A. So the number is FA, which is 15 × 16 + 10 = 250 in decimal.

questions.question: Put the parts of a proof by induction in order.
items: State the claim for every whole number n ≥ 1
Assume the claim holds for n = k
Use that assumption to prove it for n = k + 1
Conclude that the claim holds for every n ≥ 1
questions.explanation: The base case knocks over the first domino, and the inductive step shows each domino knocks over the next. Only with both in place can you conclude the claim for every n.

questions.question: Each connected graph below is described by its vertex degrees. Select every one that has an Euler path (a walk using every edge exactly once).
choices: Degrees 2, 2, 2, 2
Degrees 3, 3, 2, 2
Degrees 3, 3, 3, 3
Degrees 1, 1, 2, 2, 2
Degrees 5, 3, 3, 3
questions.explanation: A connected graph has an Euler path exactly when zero or two vertices have odd degree. 2, 2, 2, 2 has none (a cycle), while 3, 3, 2, 2 and 1, 1, 2, 2, 2 have two each. 3, 3, 3, 3 has four odd vertices, and 5, 3, 3, 3 is Königsberg itself.

questions.question: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from now?
choices: Thursday
Saturday
Tuesday
Friday
questions.explanation: Days repeat every 7, so work mod 7: 100 = 14 × 7 + 2, and 100 mod 7 = 2. Two days after Wednesday is Friday. Counting 100 mod 10 or forgetting to reduce gives the wrong offset.
